title: Pre-flight: Toolchain, Modules & the Shell
description: Optional, skippable refresher: Git, the shell, and the Go toolchain (go, modules, run/build/test).

title: Go Fundamentals: Syntax, Types & Control Flow
description: Packages, variables, the basic types, zero values, control flow, and functions — the bedrock of every Go program.

title: Structs, Methods, Interfaces & Errors
description: Structs and methods, interfaces defined by the consumer, idiomatic error handling, and slices & maps in depth.

title: Data Semantics & Data-Oriented Design
description: Value vs pointer semantics and what copying really does; struct field ordering, alignment and padding; and designing data around how it's accessed, not just modeled.

title: Concurrency: Goroutines, Channels & Select
description: Goroutines, channels, select, sync primitives, and the core concurrency patterns — with the scheduler underneath.

title: Generics in Go, In Depth
description: Type parameters, constraints and type sets, inference and its limits, and how the compiler implements generics (GC-shape stenciling + dictionaries).

title: Functional Go: Closures, Combinators & Monads
description: Functional programming the idiomatic Go way: first-class functions and closures, function composition and currying, predicate/parser/middleware combinators, generic Map/Filter/Reduce and lazy iterators (iter.Seq), and Option/Result/Either with Map/FlatMap — plus an honest account of Go's FP limits (no higher-kinded types, no tail-call optimization) and when (T, error) and a plain loop beat the monad.

title: The context Package, In Depth
description: Cancellation, deadlines and timeouts; how Done() signals; propagation through goroutine trees, HTTP and DB; values and the classic leaks.

title: The Sharp Tools: Reflection, Profiling & unsafe
description: Reflection, the profiling toolchain, and unsafe — the sharp tools, when they earn their keep, and how to wield them without bleeding.

title: Testing in Go
description: The testing package end to end: table-driven tests, subtests, benchmarks, fuzzing, the race detector, coverage, mocking, integration tests against real deps (testcontainers), httptest and golden files.

title: Test-Driven Development in Go
description: The red → green → refactor loop; writing the test first and letting it drive the design; growing a Meridian transfer validator test-by-test; table-driven TDD, test doubles via interfaces, the testing pyramid, and the honest cases where TDD helps versus where it gets in the way.

title: Project: A Real CLI Tool
description: Build a CLI that exercises everything so far — flags, I/O, errors, concurrency — shipped with a real, runnable test suite.

title: Command-Line Tools: flag, Cobra & TUIs
description: Building real CLIs in Go: the stdlib flag package in depth, Cobra for subcommands and persistent flags (the kubectl/gh pattern), urfave/cli as the alternative, Viper config integration, interactive prompts and TUIs with Bubble Tea, and generating shell completions.

title: Design Patterns, the Go Way
description: Idiomatic Go patterns — functional options, accept-interfaces/return-structs, worker pools, fan-in/out, middleware via closures — and where the GoF patterns do and don't fit.

title: Software Design & Architecture
description: SOLID mapped to Go, package design and dependency direction, hexagonal/ports-and-adapters, project layout, and designing for testability.

title: Networking & How the Web Actually Works
description: TCP/UDP and sockets, HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2, DNS, the TLS handshake, and the full journey of a request across the internet.

title: HTTP Clients
description: net/http clients done right: timeouts, transports and connection pooling, retries, context, and decoding responses safely.

title: Project: A Pokedex CLI (API Consumer)
description: Build an API-consuming app with caching and pagination — a Pokedex-style CLI — with a full test suite.

title: SQL & Databases in Go
description: database/sql and pool tuning, the pgx driver, context-aware parameterized queries and transactions, migrations (golang-migrate/goose), the sqlc vs sqlx vs ORM choice, indexing and EXPLAIN, killing N+1, and zero-downtime expand-contract migrations.

title: HTTP Servers: JSON, Streaming & WebSockets
description: Routing, middleware and handlers; advanced JSON (custom marshalers, RawMessage, omitempty, safe decoding); streaming with json.Encoder and NDJSON; and real-time with server-sent events and WebSockets.

title: Auth & API Design
description: Password hashing, sessions vs tokens, JWTs and their footguns, OAuth2/OIDC, passkeys (WebAuthn) and MFA; plus REST conventions, versioning, pagination, idempotency and OpenAPI.

title: File Servers, go:embed & CDNs
description: Serving files with http.FileServer/ServeContent, range requests and caching headers; embedding assets with go:embed and io/fs into one binary; and CDNs — edge caching, fingerprinted and signed URLs.

title: Caching & Redis
description: Why caching exists, Redis as the workhorse, cache-aside/read-through/write-through strategies, and the hard part: invalidation, stampedes and singleflight.

title: Project: A Blog Aggregator Backend
description: Tie together HTTP + SQL + auth with deliberate API design and a caching layer into a real backend service, fully tested.

title: Microservices
description: When to split a monolith, service boundaries, inter-service communication, and the operational cost microservices really carry.

title: Docker & Containerization
description: Images, layers and the build cache, multi-stage builds down to scratch/distroless, and docker compose for local multi-service development.

title: Building & Shipping Go Binaries
description: Cross-compilation with GOOS/GOARCH, the cgo/static-binary trap behind scratch images (CGO_ENABLED=0), build metadata with -ldflags and runtime/debug.ReadBuildInfo, reproducible builds, and releasing with GoReleaser.

title: Deployment & Infra: CI/CD + Kubernetes
description: From commit to production: CI/CD pipelines, reverse proxies and load balancers, and Kubernetes from first principles to rolling deploys.

title: Idiomatic Go & the Go Mindset
description: Effective Go and the proverbs; small interfaces, useful zero values, when NOT to abstract; implementing stdlib interfaces (Stringer, error, sort.Interface, io.Reader/Writer, json.Marshaler); and type assertions vs type switches.

title: Error Handling at Scale
description: Wrapping with %w, errors.Is/As, sentinel vs typed errors, when to panic, structured error responses, and the typed-nil-error trap that makes err != nil lie.

title: Context in Production
description: Real-world cancellation discipline across services, request-scoped values done right, and propagating deadlines through HTTP, gRPC and DB layers.

title: Time, Clocks & Timers
description: Monotonic vs wall clock and why durations survive NTP/DST; timers and tickers without leaks (and the Go 1.23 timer GC change); injecting a Clock interface for deterministic tests; and timezones, DST and the reference-time layout.

title: The Go Scheduler (GMP), In Depth
description: The G/M/P model, run queues and work-stealing, blocking syscalls and the netpoller, GOMAXPROCS, async preemption (1.14+) and sysmon — and why CPU-bound goroutines behave nothing like I/O-bound ones.

title: Concurrency Patterns
description: The composition vocabulary: pipelines, fan-out/fan-in, done/or-done channels, generators, tee/bridge, bounded parallelism, semaphores, errgroup, futures, confinement, heartbeats, singleflight — and when a mutex is the right tool instead.

title: Advanced Concurrency & Correctness
description: Correctness under load: backpressure, the race detector in practice, designing for zero data races, the Go memory model and happens-before, and the bugs that survive review — lost wakeups, goroutine leaks, deadlocks.

title: Project: A Concurrent Cinema Booking System
description: Build a seat-booking system and solve the double-booking race three ways: an in-memory store that fails under -race, a sync.RWMutex pessimistic-lock store that fixes it, and a Redis store (SET NX EX + PERSIST) for distributed holds — with a hold → confirm → release checkout session, DI/repository architecture, and a 100k-goroutine race test. The seat race is Meridian's two-transfers-on-one-balance race in a new skin.

title: Debugging Go
description: Delve (breakpoints, stepping, goroutine switching, remote/headless), reading panics and stack traces, full goroutine dumps and the deadlock detector, and production debugging with GODEBUG, net/http/pprof and core dumps.

title: Performance Engineering
description: pprof, benchmarking, escape analysis, cutting allocations, sync.Pool, GC tuning; mechanical sympathy (caches, cache lines, false sharing); the execution tracer (runtime/trace, go tool trace); and profile-guided optimization (default.pgo) — feeding production profiles back into the compiler.

title: Observability: Telemetry & Acting On It
description: slog, Prometheus metrics, OpenTelemetry tracing and correlation IDs — then the consumption side: SLIs/SLOs, error budgets, symptom-based alerting, dashboards, and the on-call/incident-response loop.

title: Reliability Patterns
description: Timeouts, retries with backoff and jitter, circuit breakers, graceful shutdown, health checks, idempotency, and rate limiting in depth (token vs leaky bucket, per-key, x/time/rate, distributed with Redis).

title: Background Jobs, Scheduling & Async Work
description: In-process cron and tickers; job queues (Asynq on Redis, River on Postgres); delayed/retryable jobs with backoff and dead-letters; idempotent handlers and draining shutdown; and leader election so a scheduled job fires once across replicas.

title: Application Security Baseline
description: Hostile input by default; the injection family (SQL, command, path traversal); SSRF; XSS and html/template auto-escaping; TLS and security headers; secrets out of logs; and supply-chain scanning with govulncheck.

title: Tooling & Engineering Hygiene
description: go vet, golangci-lint, go generate, build tags, Go workspaces (go work), race/coverage in CI, module versioning, private modules and the proxy (GOPRIVATE, GOAUTH, vendoring), reproducible builds, and supply-chain security (govulncheck, SBOM scanning).

title: Configuration & Secrets Management
description: 12-factor config, layering sources with documented precedence, validate-at-startup/fail-fast, the library landscape (flag/env, envconfig/koanf, Viper); then secrets — managers (Vault, cloud), rotation without redeploy, and keeping secrets out of logs and dumps.

title: Production Project Architecture
description: Wire everything into a real service: config and secret loading, dependency injection, layered/hexagonal structure, graceful lifecycle and a CI/CD-ready layout.

title: gRPC & Service-to-Service Communication
description: Protocol Buffers and schema-first workflow, the four RPC types, interceptors, status codes, deadlines over the wire, gRPC vs REST trade-offs, and gRPC gateways for HTTP/JSON.

title: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) in Go
description: MCP from first principles: JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio and Streamable HTTP, the initialize handshake and capability negotiation, exposing tools, resources and prompts, building a server and client by hand with the stdlib, then the official go-sdk — grounded in giving an AI assistant safe, typed, auditable access to the Meridian ledger.

title: Replication: Copies, Lag & Quorums
description: Keeping copies of your data in sync, explained from zero: why you replicate, single-leader vs multi-leader vs leaderless, replication lag and the stale-read problem, read-your-writes consistency, quorum reads and writes (W + R > N), and resolving conflicting writes with last-writer-wins and version vectors — all grounded in replicating Meridian's account balances.

title: Sharding: Splitting Data Across Machines
description: When one database is too small, you split the data across many machines — explained from zero: why you shard, choosing a partition key, key-range vs hash sharding, hot spots and skew, rebalancing without moving everything, routing a request to the right node, and sharding secondary indexes (local vs global) — all grounded in sharding Meridian's ledger.

title: Storage Engines: LSM-Trees vs B-Trees
description: What actually happens on disk when a database stores your data — explained from zero: the append-only log and the index trade-off, log-structured (LSM) engines with memtables, SSTables, compaction and Bloom filters, B-trees with pages, splits and the write-ahead log, how to choose between them (write amplification, sequential vs random writes), and why analytics uses column storage — all grounded in Meridian's ledger.

title: The Trouble with Distributed Systems
description: Everything that goes wrong once data lives on more than one machine — explained from zero: partial failure and why it's nondeterministic, unreliable networks (a timeout tells you almost nothing), unreliable clocks (time-of-day vs monotonic, NTP drift, why timestamps lie), process pauses that freeze a node mid-function, fencing tokens to stop zombie leaders corrupting data, and why a node must trust a majority quorum over its own judgment — grounded in Meridian paying a bank over a flaky network.

title: Consistency & Consensus
description: How unreliable machines agree on a single truth — explained from zero: linearizability (the illusion of one always-fresh copy) and why it's a recency guarantee, when you actually need it (leader election, uniqueness, no double-spend), the cost (the CAP trade-off, CP vs AP), logical clocks (Lamport, hybrid) for causal ordering, and consensus itself — agreeing on one value, total order broadcast, Raft, and the majority that makes it safe — grounded in keeping Meridian's ledger correct.

title: Representing Money — Never Use Floats
description: Integer minor units vs decimal libraries, currency types, rounding modes and where they're legally defined, and multi-currency handling.

title: Double-Entry Ledgers
description: Debits and credits, accounting invariants, append-only immutability, and modeling a ledger in Go with enforced invariants.

title: Transactions, Consistency & Sagas
description: ACID and isolation, optimistic vs pessimistic locking, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, concurrent transfers; then sagas — local transactions with compensating actions, orchestration vs choreography, and combining with the outbox.

title: Idempotency & Exactly-Once Semantics
description: Idempotency keys, deduplication, at-least-once vs exactly-once, safe payment retries, and the transactional outbox pattern.

title: Messaging & Pub/Sub Foundations
description: The broker-agnostic mental model: queues vs topics, producers/consumers, push vs pull, delivery guarantees, ordering, acks and dead-letter queues.

title: In-Process Pub/Sub: Building an Event Bus
description: Before you reach for a broker: an in-process, type-safe pub/sub event bus built from channels, generics and reflection — the actor model, total event ordering, and backpressure — grounded in decoupling Meridian's modules and read against Tailscale's production util/eventbus.

title: Event-Driven Architecture & Kafka
description: Event sourcing, CQRS, the outbox and reconciliation; then Kafka deep: topics, partitions, offsets, consumer groups, rebalancing and partition-key design.

title: Watermill — Event-Driven Go in Practice
description: The Publisher/Subscriber abstraction, messages and the Router, middleware, and implementing CQRS, event sourcing and the outbox with Watermill.

title: Integrating with External Payment Systems
description: Outbound: robust processor/bank clients with timeouts, retries, idempotency keys and circuit breakers. Inbound webhooks: HMAC signature verification, replay protection, async idempotent processing. And modeling pending → settled → failed states for slow rails.

title: Auditability & Compliance
description: Immutable audit logs, append-only event stores, time and clocks, data retention, and the engineering touchpoints of PCI-DSS / KYC / AML.

title: Batch & Large-File Processing
description: Nightly reconciliation, statement generation and bank-file ingest: NACHA/ACH fixed-width and ISO 20022 XML, streaming multi-GB files without loading them into memory, checkpointing and resumability, and idempotent re-processing.

title: Security for Financial Systems
description: Building on the Part 2 security baseline: secrets management, encryption at rest and in transit, request signing, authorization models, replay/tamper protection and handling PII.

title: Broken Access Control
description: The most-exploited vulnerability class, in Go: BOLA/IDOR and object enumeration, function- and collection-level authorization, multi-tenant isolation, the staging-mirrors-production trap, IAM poisoning and the confused deputy, error messages as reconnaissance, and how to test authorization exhaustively — grounded in a real $500K access-control bug haul against Google's API surface.

title: Resilience & Correctness Under Load
description: High availability, graceful degradation, per-account rate limiting, fraud-check hooks, and reconciliation as a safety net.

title: Fintech Capstone: A Payments & Ledger Service
description: Build a small but correct payments/ledger service: accounts, idempotent transfers, double-entry ledger, audit trail, gRPC, Watermill + Kafka, and a full fuzz/race test suite.

title: Complexity & the Go Toolbox
description: Big-O/Θ intuition, time vs space, and the Go-specific realities: slices as dynamic arrays/stacks, map[T]struct{} as the set, container/heap, sort.Slice, and generics for reusable structures.

title: Arrays & Strings: Two Pointers & Sliding Windows
description: Two pointers, sliding window, prefix sums, in-place tricks; and Go's []byte vs string vs []rune and where each bites.

title: Hashing: Frequency Maps & Sets
description: Frequency maps, dedup, grouping, and set operations with map[T]struct{}.

title: Stacks, Queues & Linked Lists
description: Slices as stacks, ring/container/list queues, hand-rolled singly/doubly linked lists, and monotonic stacks.

title: Trees & Recursion
description: Binary trees, BST invariants, DFS (pre/in/post-order) and BFS by level, recursion vs explicit stack.

title: Heaps & Priority Queues
description: container/heap in practice, top-K, merge-K, and the running median.

title: Graphs: BFS, DFS, Topo Sort & Dijkstra
description: Adjacency lists, BFS/DFS, topological sort, union-find, and shortest paths with Dijkstra.

title: Binary Search: On Data and On the Answer
description: Binary search on sorted data and on the answer space, with the off-by-one boundary discipline that kills most attempts.

title: Backtracking
description: Permutations, combinations, subsets, N-queens, and pruning the decision tree.

title: Dynamic Programming
description: Memoization vs tabulation, 1-D and 2-D tables, and classics: knapsack, LCS, edit distance, coin change.

title: Greedy, Intervals & Bit Manipulation
description: Interval scheduling/merging, greedy-vs-DP intuition, and the common bit tricks.

title: Interview Craft
description: Pattern recognition, narrating your approach, on-the-spot complexity analysis, and writing clean, correct, idiomatic Go under time pressure.

title: Go Mistakes: Organization & API Design
description: The first cluster of common Go mistakes — the ones that quietly rot a codebase: variable shadowing, deep nesting, init misuse, interface pollution and where to declare interfaces, why `any` says nothing, generics misuse, type-embedding traps, the functional options pattern, and package/tooling hygiene — each shown as the bug, the why, and the idiomatic fix.

title: Go Mistakes: Data, Slices & Maps
description: The data-type mistakes that don't just read badly — they lose or corrupt data: integer overflow and float imprecision, slice length vs capacity, nil vs empty slices, the append that silently clobbers a shared backing array, slice and map memory leaks that pin megabytes, map initialization, and comparing values correctly (== vs slices.Equal vs reflect.DeepEqual).

title: Go Mistakes: Control Flow & Strings
description: Control-flow and string mistakes that quietly break correctness: how range loops copy elements (so your mutation vanishes), how range arguments are evaluated once up front, pointer-of-loop-variable traps, map iteration order and insert-during-iteration, labelled break, defer inside a loop piling up resources; then strings — runes vs bytes, correct UTF-8 iteration, trim-function misuse, efficient concatenation with strings.Builder, useless conversions, and substrings that leak the whole backing string.

title: Go Mistakes: Functions, Methods & Errors
description: Function, method, and error-handling mistakes: choosing value vs pointer receivers, named result parameters and their deferred-mutation side effects, the typed-nil receiver that makes err != nil lie, taking an io.Reader instead of a filename, how defer evaluates its arguments and receiver up front; then error management — when to panic, wrapping with %w, checking with errors.Is/errors.As instead of ==/type assertion, not handling an error twice, and not swallowing deferred Close errors.

title: Go Mistakes: Concurrency
description: The concurrency mistakes that cause the worst production bugs: confusing concurrency with parallelism, assuming concurrency is always faster, choosing channels vs mutexes, data races vs race conditions and the Go memory model, context propagation and cancellation, goroutine leaks, nondeterministic select, notification and nil channels, channel sizing, WaitGroup and sync.Cond misuse, errgroup, data races from append, and the copied-mutex trap that go vet catches.

title: Go Mistakes: Standard Library, Testing & Optimizations
description: The final cluster of Go mistakes: standard-library traps (time.Duration units, time.After allocation churn, JSON and SQL pitfalls, unclosed HTTP/SQL/file resources, missing return after http.Error, timeout-less default HTTP client and server), testing mistakes (categorizing tests, the -race flag, table-driven tests, not sleeping, injecting a clock, httptest, accurate benchmarks), and optimization fundamentals (CPU caches and false sharing, struct alignment, stack vs heap and escape analysis, reducing allocations, inlining, pprof and the tracer, the GC, and running Go in containers with a container-aware GOMAXPROCS).

title: OWASP Top 10: A Bug-Hunter's Field Guide
description: The OWASP Top 10 from the attacker's side of the table: one real, publicly documented breach or bounty per category — First American (IDOR, 885M files), Adobe (3DES-ECB passwords), Heartland (SQL injection), Starbucks (race-condition design flaw), Tesla (open Kubernetes console), Equifax (CVE-2017-5638), Instagram (rate-limit bypass), event-stream (npm supply chain), Target (ignored alerts), Capital One (SSRF to cloud metadata) — each paired with the Go pattern that defends against it and the bug-hunter's recon-and-test methodology.

title: Building Security Tooling in Go
description: Why Go is the language of the recon toolchain (nuclei, httpx, ffuf, subfinder are all Go), and how to build your own for authorized testing: a bounded concurrent HTTP prober with a worker pool, an in-scope guard so you never touch an unauthorized host, a token-bucket rate limiter, response classification, and the authorization-matrix fuzzer that automates the two-user test against your own API — every example hermetic and runnable with httptest.

title: Project: A DNS Resolver
description: Build a DNS resolver from scratch in Go: model A/AAAA/CNAME/MX/TXT records and a zone store, resolve names through the lookup chain, add a TTL cache that expires entries, validate records, detect CNAME cycles, serve a zone transfer (AXFR-style), and format results dig-style — every stage runnable and stdlib-only.

title: TLS Fingerprinting & Browser Impersonation
description: Demystified from the bytes up: why a Go HTTP client is identifiable before it sends a single header, the TLS ClientHello and how JA3 (MD5 of cipher/extension/curve lists) and JA4 (sorted, SHA-256, GREASE-stripped) hash it into a fingerprint, the HTTP/2 Akamai fingerprint (SETTINGS frame + pseudo-header order), how uTLS forges an arbitrary ClientHello before crypto/tls sees it, and how bogdanfinn/tls-client and enetx/surf assemble browser-accurate fingerprints — for authorized testing, scraping-defense research, and understanding anti-bot systems.

title: Inside the Impersonation Stack: uTLS, tls-client & surf
description: The source code, line by line: the TLSExtension interface (Len/Read/writeToUConn) every uTLS extension implements, how SupportedCurvesExtension serializes to exact wire bytes, the real Chrome ClientHelloSpec explained extension by extension, the build pipeline (buildHandshakeState → applyPresetByID → ApplyConfig → MarshalClientHello), extension shuffling, tls-client's ClientProfile struct that bundles the TLS and HTTP/2 fingerprints, and surf's Impersonate/applyVariant — with runnable stdlib re-implementations that emit genuine ClientHello bytes.

title: Time, Backoff & Jitter: Retrying Without Making It Worse
description: The deep, source-grounded treatment of retry timing: measuring elapsed time with the monotonic clock (and the Go 1.23 timer GC change so retry loops don't leak), capped exponential backoff, the thundering herd, the full jitter taxonomy from the AWS backoff study (no jitter / full / equal / decorrelated) with the simulation result, retry budgets and retry amplification across tiers, context deadline propagation, and a production retry loop that combines decorrelated jitter, a deadline, a budget, and idempotency — every algorithm runnable in stdlib.

title: Bug Bounty Recon & Methodology
description: The hunting workflow grounded in 6,400+ real disclosed writeups: attack-surface mapping (subdomain enumeration, content/endpoint discovery, JavaScript analysis for hidden routes and keys), the hunt loop (map → probe → escalate → chain), choosing targets by bug-class ROI, triage and severity (CVSS), and writing the report that gets paid — with runnable stdlib Go recon helpers. Authorized-testing only.

title: High-Value Bug Classes: ATO, Race, SSRF & Logic
description: The recurring money-makers from the writeup corpus, each demystified with real disclosed cases and runnable Go: race conditions (TOCTOU, limit-overrun on withdrawals), account takeover (OAuth redirect_uri, password-reset token flaws, pre-account-takeover), SSRF chains to cloud metadata (IMDSv1 vs IMDSv2), subdomain takeover (dangling DNS), and business-logic flaws. Defensive framing — the Go server-side fixes for each.

title: The Case Bank: Real Disclosed Bugs by Class
description: A curated reference of real, publicly-disclosed bug bounty writeups mined from the pentester.land corpus (6,400+ reports), grouped by vulnerability class — each with the bounty, target, source link, and the one-line lesson. A study index that maps every class in this security track to the real-world reports that prove it.

title: API Recon & Abuse at Scale: Lessons from the Google Hunts
description: Advanced API attack techniques from real disclosed Google hunts (brutecat): API discovery and ProtoJSON schema-fuzzing oracles, ID-to-PII over-disclosure (obfuscated ID → email), enumeration at scale (IP rate-limit bypass via IPv6 /64 rotation + masked-value oracles), IDOR UUID extraction by binary search over filter operators, notification suppression via unbounded fields, and the disclosure→IDOR→privilege-escalation chain to RCE — each with a runnable Go demo and the server-side fix. Defensive framing.

title: CORS: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing, From Zero
description: CORS explained from absolute zero — assuming no prior knowledge. The same-origin policy and what an 'origin' actually is (scheme + host + port), why the browser blocks cross-origin reads, what CORS is and the exact header negotiation it runs, simple vs preflighted (OPTIONS) requests, every CORS response header (Allow-Origin/Methods/Headers/Credentials/Max-Age/Vary), the credentials-and-cookies story and why '*' + credentials is forbidden, the misconfigurations that become account takeover (reflected origin, null origin, suffix/regex matching), a correct Go CORS middleware built step by step, and where CORS does NOT protect you — every server-side piece runnable and verified.

title: Real-Time Go: WebSocket Hubs & Outbound Webhooks
description: The producer side of real-time Go, built end to end: the WebSocket Hub pattern (one goroutine owning the client set; register/unregister/broadcast over channels; per-client send buffers and slow-client drop so one stalled connection can't block the fan-out; ping/pong keepalives) for pushing live events to many clients; and outbound webhooks (signing the payload with HMAC-SHA256, delivering with retries + exponential backoff + jitter, dead-lettering after exhaustion, and at-least-once delivery that forces the receiver to dedup). Complements the single-connection WebSocket section (ch19) and the inbound-webhook verification section (ch9). Every server-side piece runnable and verified.

title: Golings: The Fix-It Track
description: A rustlings-style track for Go, in the browser: an ordered set of tiny BROKEN programs you fix in the page and run on the real Go sandbox. Each exercise passes only when your fix compiles cleanly and prints the expected output — real pass/fail, not a simulation. Progress is saved as you go. Covers the core reflexes: variables, types and conversion, functions, slices and append, maps, structs and pointers, methods and pointer receivers, interfaces, errors as values, closures, goroutines with WaitGroup, and channels.

title: Request-Level Attacks: Smuggling, Host Header & Cache Poisoning
description: The PortSwigger-class attacks that exploit how proxies, caches, and origin servers DISAGREE about a single HTTP request — explained from the bytes up, Go-grounded. HTTP request smuggling (CL.TE / TE.CL desync, and an empirical look at how strictly Go's net/http parses ambiguous Content-Length / Transfer-Encoding so a Go origin doesn't disagree with itself); Host header attacks (password-reset poisoning, routing and cache off a forgeable r.Host, with the allowlist/configured-base-URL fix); and web cache poisoning (reflecting an unkeyed input like X-Forwarded-Host into a cached response that's then served to every victim). Every server-side behavior runnable and verified.

title: Burp Suite: How It Works & How to Use It
description: The web hacker's primary tool, explained from the mechanism up — Go-grounded. What Burp Suite is (an intercepting proxy plus an attack toolkit), and HOW interception actually works: Burp is a man-in-the-middle proxy that sits between your browser and the target, reading and modifying every request — demonstrated with a runnable Go intercepting proxy that rewrites a request in flight, plus the TLS story (Burp's own CA certificate, why you install it, and what that means). Then each tool and when to reach for it: Proxy + intercept and the sitemap/scope, Repeater (the manual probe workhorse for IDOR/auth/logic bugs), Intruder (automated payloads — sniper/battering-ram/pitchfork/cluster-bomb), Decoder/Inspector, Comparer, Sequencer, and the Scanner (Pro). Ends with the practical hunting workflow and how each Bible attack class maps onto Burp. Authorized testing only.

title: HTTP Response Headers You Must Get Right: Caching, Cookies & Security Headers
description: The response envelope, from zero. A single Go HTTP response is a body wrapped in instructions to the browser and every cache between you and it. Assumes no prior knowledge: what an HTTP header is and how net/http reads/writes them (Set vs Add, canonicalization, the set-after-WriteHeader gotcha, default headers, content sniffing); the caching family (the full Cache-Control vocabulary, ETag/If-None-Match 304 revalidation, Vary); the cookie family (the http.Cookie struct and every attribute, the __Host- prefix, the unset-SameSite-is-Lax gotcha); and the security headers Go sets NONE of by default (CSP, HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy). Ends with a reusable secureHeaders middleware. Every header behavior measured against go1.24.

title: OAuth 2.1 & OpenID Connect from the Ground Up: Flows, PKCE, and the Protection Map
description: Delegated auth the way the developer who built it sees it. Builds on the sessions/JWT/cookie foundations (ch20) and goes deep on the OAuth/OIDC half: authentication vs authorization; OAuth's four roles and two tokens; refresh-token rotation with reuse detection; the six-step Authorization Code Flow and its back-channel client_secret; exact redirect_uri matching vs the loose-match bug; PKCE (verifier->challenge, S256 vs plain, the downgrade); the four other flows and which are deprecated; OAuth 2.1's hardening; JWT validation and the alg-confusion seam (alg:none); OIDC id_token vs access_token and the email_verified account-takeover; and the Protection Map. Every mechanism is a runnable, go1.24-verified stdlib Go demo.

title: The Bug Bounty Income Playbook: From Zero to a Steady $300+/Month
description: The honest, sourced strategy for turning this security track into modest, repeatable bug-bounty income. The realistic earnings timeline (months 1-3 = $0; $300/mo reachable around month 4-8) and why income is lumpy; why IDOR/broken access control is the one class to master first and its read->write->vertical payout ladder, with a runnable Go model of the Autorize/Authz replay-and-diff detection; recon as 60-80% of the job (subfinder->httpx->JS-mining->nuclei->anew); low-hanging fruit (info disclosure, subdomain takeover, JWT alg:none, CORS); picking programs/platforms (the VDP->public->private-invite ladder, higher-minimum-bounty selection); reports that get paid (the five-part structure); and an 8-week plan cross-linked to the chapters that teach each skill. Income figures are community-reported ranges, not guarantees.
